title: Choosing a Collection for a Problem
learningObjectives: Translate a task into data-collection requirements.
Compare sequence, set, map, stack, queue, and nested collection behaviors.
Choose a collection using ordering, duplicates, lookup, update, and grouping requirements.
Explain why performance depends on operations, implementation, and data size.
Review a collection choice when requirements or constraints change.

understand.concept: Collection choice begins with behavior, not syntax. Ask whether order must be preserved, duplicates are meaningful, items are identified by position or key, values are added or removed at particular ends, or data is grouped. Each structure makes some operations natural and others less convenient. A collection can be technically usable yet poorly matched to the task.
understand.whyItMatters: A structure that does not express the requirements clearly can cause duplicate records, awkward lookup code, ordering bugs, or unnecessary work. Choosing intentionally improves correctness and makes the design easier to explain and change.
understand.analogy: Think of storage tools: trays keep items in a sequence, labeled drawers help find something by label, and a checklist can represent unique entries. Choose the storage style that matches how you will use the contents.
understand.analogyLimit: Programming collections have language-specific APIs, equality rules, ordering guarantees, and performance trade-offs. Everyday storage analogies help orient learners but do not replace technical documentation.

explain.narrative: Before choosing, list operations the program will perform most often. A sequence fits ordered items where duplicates may matter. A set fits uniqueness. A map/dictionary fits lookup by a meaningful key. A stack fits last-in-first-out processing, and a queue fits first-in-first-out processing. Nested collections fit groups or multi-level data. Check edge cases—empty data, duplicate values, missing keys, and invalid indexes. Do not claim one structure is universally fastest: complexity and real performance depend on language, implementation, operation, and scale. If the requirements change, reconsider the structure.

examples.title: Ordered list with duplicates
examples.explanation: A sequence keeps order and repeated entries, useful when duplicates are meaningful.

examples.title: Uniqueness is required
examples.explanation: A Set expresses uniqueness, so adding the same value does not create a second distinct member.

examples.title: Find by key
examples.explanation: A map associates a stable product code with its quantity; the code can retrieve the value using that key.

examples.title: FIFO processing
examples.explanation: Removing the first item models first-in-first-out order. A queue abstraction is clearer if this behavior is central to the program.

examples.title: Grouped information
examples.explanation: A keyed grouping with inner sequences associates values with a group and supports access within that group.

commonMistakes: Picking a collection because its syntax is familiar rather than based on required behavior.
Using a sequence when uniqueness must be enforced and then duplicating deduplication logic in many places.
Using fragile numeric positions for items that have stable identities.
Assuming all collections have the same ordering or performance guarantees.
Over-nesting data where a flat structure would be clearer.
Forgetting missing keys, empty collections, duplicates, and boundary cases when designing access.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Match data needs to collection behavior
guidedTask.instructions: Choose a structure for each situation and justify it with the requirement that matters most.
steps: A playlist must preserve order and allow repeated tracks—choose and explain.
A set of unique tags must avoid duplicate entries—choose and explain.
Product quantities must be found by product code—choose and explain.
Incoming jobs must be processed oldest-first—choose and explain.
A timetable groups several entries by day—choose a suitable grouped structure and describe its shape.
guidedTask.starterCode: // For each scenario, record: key requirements -> structure -> reason -> edge case.

independentTask.title: Independent: Data structure design note
independentTask.instructions: Create a short design for a library, event-registration, game-inventory, or travel-planning scenario.
requirements: State at least four data requirements (order, duplicates, lookup, grouping, or removal behavior).
Select at least two collection types for different parts of the model and justify each.
Show a representative operation for each selection using pseudocode or code.
Identify one edge case such as empty data, duplicate input, missing key, or invalid index.
Describe a changed requirement that would make you reconsider a selection.

hints: Write down the required behavior before choosing a type.
Order and uniqueness are different properties—decide about each separately.
Use set-like behavior when uniqueness is a core rule.
Use key-value structures when lookup is by a stable identifier.
Stack or queue behavior is useful when processing/removal order is a requirement.
Nested structures can preserve group relationships; avoid unnecessary nesting.
Performance claims should specify operation, implementation, and scale.

questions.prompt: A playlist must preserve order and may contain the same song more than once. Which behavior best fits?
options: A key-value map without sequence order
questions.explanation: Sequences preserve order and can retain repeated entries.

questions.prompt: A program must keep each visited page only once. Which collection is the clearest fit?
questions.explanation: The primary requirement is uniqueness, which set-like collections express directly.

questions.prompt: Stock quantity is retrieved using a product code. Which structure naturally models this?
options: A sequence searched only by position
questions.explanation: The product code is a key linked to its quantity.

questions.prompt: Which statement about collection performance is accurate?
options: It depends on the implementation, operation, and scale
Every map is always faster than every sequence
All collection types have identical performance
questions.answer: It depends on the implementation, operation, and scale
questions.explanation: Performance varies by implementation, data size, and operation; blanket claims are misleading.

questions.prompt: If requirements change so repeated entries must be removed, what should a developer do?
options: Reassess the collection choice and uniqueness handling
Keep duplicates and hide them during display
questions.answer: Reassess the collection choice and uniqueness handling
questions.explanation: Collection design should reflect the current requirements and constraints.
